html:
The script of the Armenian language, created around 405 by the monk and scholar Mesrop Mashtots, with the support of the head of the church, Sahak, and the Armenian king. It began with 36 letters; two more were added in the Middle Ages.

Armenia had adopted Christianity about a century before, but church services and scripture were in Greek or Syriac, which most people did not understand. Mashtots made a letter for every sound of Armenian. The first text written in it was a line from the Book of Proverbs, and his team then translated the Bible.

A burst of writing followed in the 5th century, with histories, translations and sermons. The alphabet gave Armenians a written culture of their own, which held them together under Persian, Arab, Byzantine, Turkish and Russian rule. It is still used today, almost unchanged. Tradition also credits Mashtots with the first Georgian alphabet.
